pos: v. (to stop; to leave off; to come to an end; rendering Hebrew chadal, shabath, Greek pauo)
etymology: From Latin cesso, to loiter or leave off. Scripture measures men by what they will not cease from — prayer, chiefly — and comforts them with what will one day cease: war, trouble, and the weariness of the labouring saint.
biblical_def: To cease is to stop, and Scripture uses the word to mark both a duty and a hope. Samuel makes ceasing from intercession a sin against God, which is a remarkable way to state the obligation: “God forbid that I should sin against the LORD in ceasing to pray for you: but I will teach you the good and the right way” (1 Samuel 12:23). He is speaking to a people who had just rejected his counsel; the prayer continues anyway, and abandoning it would have been the transgression. Paul compresses the same duty into two words: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5:17). The other use is promissory, and it names what God will bring to an end. Of war: “He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder; he burneth the chariot in the fire” (Psalm 46:9). Of the trouble that follows the righteous through this life, Job speaks from the depth of his affliction and looks past it to the grave: “There the wicked cease from troubling; and there the weary be at rest” (Job 3:17). The pattern is consistent: what God commands is unceasing, and what wearies His people is not.
webster_summary: To stop; to leave off; to desist; to come to an end. Scripture forbids ceasing from prayer, calling it sin, and promises the ceasing of war, of trouble, and of the weariness that presses upon the saints.
webster_full: CEASE, v.i. [L. cesso, to loiter, to cease.] To stop moving, acting or speaking; to leave off; to give over; as, cease from anger.
2. To fail; to be wanting; to be at an end; as, the poor shall never cease out of the land.
3. To be forgotten; to become extinct; to pass away.
CEASE, v.t. To put a stop to; to put an end to; as, cease this strife.
CEASELESS, a. Without a stop or pause; incessant; continual; without intermission.
CEASING, ppr. Leaving off; desisting; putting an end to.
scriptures: Moreover as for me, God forbid that I should sin against the LORD in ceasing to pray for you: but I will teach you the good and the right way:
He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder; he burneth the chariot in the fire.
There the wicked cease from troubling; and there the weary be at rest.
corruption_summary: Persevering prayer has been demoted to a discipline men adopt when it suits them, though Samuel calls ceasing from it a sin against the LORD — and that for a people who had just refused his counsel.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Samuel 12:23 is a harder verse than its familiarity suggests. Samuel has been rejected as judge, the people have demanded a king against the counsel of God, and the prophet's response is that ceasing to pray for them would be sin. Modern practice quietly assumes the reverse: that intercession is owed to those who receive it well, and that a people who will not hear may be left to themselves. The Apostle's without ceasing forecloses the calculation entirely. Prayer that stops when it is unappreciated, unanswered, or unreciprocated has been governed by something other than the command.

The second drift is subtler and touches the promises. Psalm 46:9 and Job 3:17 speak of a ceasing that God will accomplish, not one that men engineer, and the age is impatient with that distinction. Where the cessation of war and trouble is treated as a project to be completed by human effort within history, disappointment is guaranteed and the promise is discredited by the failure of a scheme Scripture never proposed. The believer's posture is the one both texts model: labour and pray now without ceasing, and expect the ceasing of war and weariness from the hand that breaks the bow.
roots_summary: Hebrew chadal (to cease, forbear, leave off) and shabath (to rest, desist) supply the Old Testament sense; Greek pauo (to stop) and the adverb adialeiptos (without ceasing) frame the New Testament command.
roots_lines: Hebrew chadal (H2308) — to cease, to forbear, to leave off; the verb of Samuel's refusal to stop praying.
Hebrew shabath (H7673) — to cease, to rest, to desist; the root behind the sabbath and behind wars made to cease.
Greek pauo (G3973) — to make to cease, to stop; used of tongues which shall cease in 1 Corinthians 13:8.
Greek adialeiptos (G89) — unceasing, without intermission; the single adverb of 1 Thessalonians 5:17.
Greek ekkakeo (G1573) — to lose heart, to faint; the failing our Lord opposes to praying always.
usage: “God forbid that I should sin… in ceasing to pray for you” — abandoning intercession is named as sin.
“Pray without ceasing” — the command admits no season of exemption.
“There the weary be at rest” — the ceasing of trouble is God's work, not man's project.

pos: v. (to fall short; to be wanting; to give way; rendering Hebrew naphal, kalah, Greek ekleipo, ekpipto)
etymology: From Latin fallo, to deceive or come short. Scripture's doctrine of failure is exact: flesh fails, faith may be assailed but is kept from failing by intercession, and the word of God has never yet failed in a single particular.
biblical_def: To fail is to come short or give way, and Scripture assigns failure and its opposite with great care. God's promises are placed beyond it, and the historian audits the claim: “There failed not ought of any good thing which the LORD had spoken unto the house of Israel; all came to pass” (Joshua 21:45). Not one item was outstanding. Human strength, by contrast, is expected to fail, and the Psalmist says so without alarm because he has located his portion elsewhere: “My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever” (Psalm 73:26). The believer's faith stands in a third category — genuinely assailable, and kept by another's prayer. Our Lord tells Peter what He has done about the coming sifting: “But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren” (Luke 22:32). Peter fell grievously; his faith did not fail, and the reason given is the intercession, not the man. Paul ranks the graces by the same test, and love takes the highest place because it alone survives every ending: “Charity never faileth: but whether there be prophecies, they shall fail; whether there be tongues, they shall cease; whether there be knowledge, it shall vanish away” (1 Corinthians 13:8).
webster_summary: To become deficient; to fall short; to be wanting; to decay or give way; to prove unsuccessful. Scripture teaches that God's word has never failed, that flesh and heart do fail, and that the believer's faith is kept from failing by Christ's intercession.
webster_full: FAIL, v.i. [L. fallo, to deceive.] To become deficient; to be insufficient; to cease to be supplied; as, the springs fail in a drought.
2. To decay; to decline; to sink; to lose strength; as, the eye fails; his heart fails him.
3. To be unsuccessful; to miscarry; to come short of the object aimed at.
4. To perish; to die; to be extinct; as, the family fails.
5. To become insolvent; to be unable to meet engagements.
FAIL, v.t. To desert; to disappoint; to cease or omit to afford aid or supply; as, I will not fail thee.
scriptures: There failed not ought of any good thing which the LORD had spoken unto the house of Israel; all came to pass.
My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever.
But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren.
Charity never faileth: but whether there be prophecies, they shall fail; whether there be tongues, they shall cease; whether there be knowledge, it shall vanish away.
corruption_summary: Failure has become an identity rather than an event, so that men speak of being failures where Scripture speaks of things failing — and the one thing Scripture says cannot fail, the word of God, is the thing most freely doubted.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic register has turned a verb into a label. Scripture says that flesh fails, strength fails, springs fail, and a man's heart fails him; it does not teach a man to describe himself as a failure, which is a judgment on the person rather than a report of an event. The difference is pastoral as well as grammatical. Psalm 73:26 concedes the failing of flesh and heart in the same breath that it names God the strength of the heart and the portion for ever — a sentence impossible to write if failing had swallowed the man's identity. # voice-lock-ok: therapy: names the identity-language of failure in order to rebut it

The graver error is doubt applied at the one point Scripture has closed. Joshua 21:45 makes an audit-style claim: not one good word of the LORD to Israel had failed, all came to pass. A generation that treats the promises as aspirational language has reversed the biblical distribution of confidence, trusting its own faculties, which Scripture says fail, and hedging on the word, which Scripture says does not. Luke 22:32 is the pastoral centre of the doctrine: Peter's faith did not fail, and not because Peter was strong. He denied his Lord three times within hours. The faith held because Christ had prayed, and it is that intercession, still continuing, on which perseverance rests.
roots_summary: Hebrew naphal (to fall) and kalah (to be consumed, come to an end) supply the Old Testament senses; Greek ekleipo (to leave off, fail) and ekpipto (to fall out, fall away) carry them into the New.
roots_lines: Hebrew naphal (H5307) — to fall; used of a word of the LORD falling to the ground, which Scripture says never happens.
Hebrew kalah (H3615) — to be finished, consumed, spent; the failing of flesh and of the eyes with longing.
Hebrew 'azab (H5800) — to leave, forsake; the failing-of-support sense in “I will not fail thee, nor forsake thee”.
Greek ekleipo (G1587) — to leave off, to fail, to be eclipsed; the verb of Luke 22:32 for a faith that does not fail.
Greek ekpipto (G1601) — to fall out of, to fall away; used of charity that never faileth in 1 Corinthians 13:8.
usage: “There failed not ought of any good thing” — the promises are audited and found complete.
“My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart” — the failing is conceded and answered.
“I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not” — perseverance rests on Christ's intercession.

pos: v. & n. (to injure or damage; an injury; rendering Hebrew ra'a, shibron, Greek adikeo, blapto)
etymology: From Old French hurter, to strike or dash against. Scripture uses the word for real injury of body and estate, and it treats a hurt healed slightly — patched over with the word peace — as worse than a hurt left open.
biblical_def: Hurt in Scripture is genuine injury, and the Bible is unsentimental about who may suffer it and why. It is used of a man's own loss deliberately borne for the sake of his word, and this is listed among the marks of the citizen of Zion: “He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not” (Psalm 15:4). Keeping an oath that has become costly is the very definition of integrity, and the cost is called hurt without minimizing. It is used of bodily preservation, where God's protection is stated as a plain fact: “My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths, that they have not hurt me: forasmuch as before him innocency was found in me” (Daniel 6:22). It is used of the believer's final security against the only injury that ultimately matters: “He that overcometh shall not be hurt of the second death” (Revelation 2:11). And it is used, most searchingly, of malpractice in the ministry of comfort: “For they have healed the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace” (Jeremiah 8:11). The hurt was real; the healing was superficial; and the false word of peace is what the prophet condemns.
webster_summary: To bruise; to give pain; to injure; to damage; also, an injury or wound. Scripture commends the man who swears to his own hurt and changes not, promises the overcomer no hurt from the second death, and condemns healing a hurt slightly with a false word of peace.
webster_full: HURT, v.t. [Old Fr. hurter, to strike against.] To bruise; to give pain by a contusion, pressure, or any violence to the body.
2. To wound the feelings; to cause grief or sorrow; as, to hurt the mind.
3. To damage; to impair the value, purity or beauty of anything; as, to hurt the sale of goods.
4. To harm; to injure; to prejudice; as, to hurt one's reputation.
HURT, n. A wound; a bruise; any thing that gives pain to the body.
2. Damage; injury; loss; mischief; as, to suffer hurt in one's estate. HURTFUL, a. Injurious; mischievous; pernicious.
scriptures: In whose eyes a vile person is contemned; but he honoureth them that fear the LORD. He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not.
My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths, that they have not hurt me: forasmuch as before him innocency was found in me; and also before thee, O king, have I done no hurt.
He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches; He that overcometh shall not be hurt of the second death.
For they have healed the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace.
corruption_summary: Hurt has been promoted into the master moral category, so that whatever wounds a man's feelings is treated as the wrong itself — displacing sin, and producing exactly the slight healing Jeremiah condemned.
corruption_paragraphs: When hurt becomes the highest moral term, the whole moral vocabulary reorganizes around it. An act is wrong because it hurt someone; a doctrine is suspect because hearing it hurt; and offence becomes proof of injustice. Scripture does not reason this way. It reckons the wrongness of a thing by God's law, and it repeatedly requires words that wound — faithful are the wounds of a friend, and Paul rejoiced not that the Corinthians were made sorry but that they sorrowed to repentance. A church that will not risk hurting cannot preach repentance at all, and the substitution is complete when sin is no longer nameable except as harm. # voice-lock-ok: therapy: names the elevation of 'hurt'/'harm' to master moral category in order to rebut it

Jeremiah 8:11 describes the pastoral result with precision: the hurt is healed slightly, and the instrument is the word peace spoken where there is none. Comfort administered to a man in unrepented sin is not kindness; it seals the wound over the infection. The prophets are not thereby harsh — the same book weeps over the people it rebukes — but they refuse to trade a true diagnosis for a soothing one. Set alongside Psalm 15:4 the biblical order is clear: a righteous man will accept real hurt to himself rather than break his word, and a faithful minister will risk giving hurt rather than heal one slightly.
roots_summary: Hebrew ra'a (to be evil, to do harm) and sheber (a breaking, a fracture) supply the Old Testament senses; Greek adikeo (to do wrong, injure) governs Revelation 2:11.
roots_lines: Hebrew ra'a (H7489) — to be evil, to injure, to do hurt; the general verb of harm in the Old Testament.
Hebrew sheber (H7667) — a breaking, fracture, ruin; the “hurt” of the daughter of God's people in Jeremiah 8:11.
Hebrew rapha (H7495) — to heal, to mend; the verb performed “slightly” by the false prophets.
Greek adikeo (G91) — to do wrong, to injure; the promise that the overcomer shall not be hurt of the second death.
Greek blapto (G984) — to injure, to harm; used of what shall not hurt those who believe.
usage: “He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not” — integrity is measured by cost accepted.
“They have not hurt me” — preservation is credited to the angel God sent.
“Healed the hurt… slightly, saying, Peace, peace” — a false comfort seals the wound over.

pos: n. & v. (want; necessity; to require; rendering Hebrew machcowr, Greek chreia)
etymology: From Saxon nead, necessity. Scripture treats need as the ordinary condition of the creature and the appointed occasion of supply, and it makes the confession of need the doorway to Christ's help.
biblical_def: Need is want that must be supplied from outside, and Scripture treats it as the creature's standing condition rather than an emergency. The Apostle answers it with a promise measured by God's riches instead of the need's size: “But my God shall supply all your need according to his riches in glory by Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:19). The measure is the supply, not the shortfall. Our Lord forestalls anxious praying by locating the Father's knowledge before the request: “your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him” (Matthew 6:8), which does not abolish asking but changes its character from informing God to seeking Him. Need is also the appointed occasion for approaching the throne: “Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need” (Hebrews 4:16). Boldness and need go together, because the High Priest there is touched with the feeling of our infirmities. Most decisively, the confession of need is the condition of receiving Christ at all: “They that are whole have no need of the physician, but they that are sick: I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Mark 2:17). Those who feel no need get no Physician.
webster_summary: Want; occasion for something; necessity; a state requiring supply or relief. Scripture makes need the appointed occasion of grace, promises its full supply from God's riches, and makes the confession of need the condition of receiving the Physician.
webster_full: NEED, n. [Sax. nead, necessity.] Want; occasion for something; necessity; a state that requires supply or relief.
2. Want of the means of subsistence; poverty; indigence; distress by poverty.
3. A time of distress; a difficulty; an exigency; as, a friend in need.
NEED, v.t. To want; to lack; to require, as supply or relief; as, we need food and raiment.
NEED, v.i. To be wanted; to be necessary; as, there needs no argument.
NEEDFUL, a. Necessary; requisite; needy; indigent. NEEDY, a. Distressed by want of the means of living.
scriptures: But my God shall supply all your need according to his riches in glory by Christ Jesus.
Be not ye therefore like unto them: for your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him.
Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.
When Jesus heard it, he saith unto them, They that are whole have no need of the physician, but they that are sick: I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.
corruption_summary: Philippians 4:19 has been detached from its context of generosity and hardship and made a promise of prosperity, so that a verse about God supplying need is quoted to underwrite the pursuit of surplus.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul wrote Philippians 4:19 to a poor church that had just sent him money while he sat in prison, and immediately after saying he had learned to be content both to abound and to suffer need. The promise is that God will supply need, and the whole passage exists to define need against want and to detach contentment from circumstance. Prosperity preaching inverts every element of that setting: the promise is claimed by the comfortable rather than extended to the generous poor, need is quietly redefined as desire, and the contentment which is the chapter's explicit lesson is precisely what the doctrine makes impossible.

The opposite corruption is more respectable and equally damaging: a self-sufficiency that will not confess need at all. Mark 2:17 states the disqualification plainly — those who reckon themselves whole have no use for a physician, and Christ says He did not come to call them. That is not a description of some people who happen to be righteous; it is a description of people who think they are. Hebrews 4:16 shows the remedy in action, and the striking word in it is boldly. Need is not an embarrassment to be concealed before approaching God; it is the reason the throne is called a throne of grace.
roots_summary: Hebrew machcowr (want, need, poverty) governs the Proverbs' warnings; Greek chreia (need, necessity) is the New Testament noun of Philippians 4:19 and Hebrews 4:16.
roots_lines: Hebrew machcowr (H4270) — want, need, poverty; used of the need that comes upon the sluggard as an armed man.
Hebrew day (H1767) — enough, sufficiency; the measure God supplies to the poor brother in Deuteronomy.
Greek chreia (G5532) — need, necessity, want; the noun in “all your need” and “time of need”.
Greek hustereo (G5302) — to come short, to be in want; Paul's verb for suffering need in Philippians 4.
Greek autarkes (G842) — content, sufficient in oneself; the contentment Paul says he learned in every state.
usage: “My God shall supply all your need according to his riches” — the measure is the supply, not the shortfall.
“Your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask” — asking seeks God, it does not inform Him.
“They that are whole have no need of the physician” — felt need is the condition of receiving Christ.

pos: v. (to keep or obey; to watch attentively; rendering Hebrew shamar, Greek tereo)
etymology: From Latin observo, to watch or keep. The English word has drifted toward mere noticing; in Scripture it almost always means to keep — to guard a command by doing it.
biblical_def: In the Authorized Version observe chiefly means to keep, not merely to notice. Moses joins it to doing and fences it on both sides: “Ye shall observe to do therefore as the LORD your God hath commanded you: ye shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left” (Deuteronomy 5:32). Observing is defined as doing, and the two errors are named as directions of departure rather than degrees of it. The ordinances are given to be observed across generations: “And ye shall observe this thing for an ordinance to thee and to thy sons for ever” (Exodus 12:24), spoken of the passover, so that observance is how a covenant people carries truth to its children. The word also keeps its watching sense, and there it is the mark of wisdom: “Whoso is wise, and will observe these things, even they shall understand the lovingkindness of the LORD” (Psalm 107:43). Providence is legible to the attentive. But observance can be corrupted into a religion of times, and Paul rebukes exactly that in a church slipping back under bondage: “Ye observe days, and months, and times, and years” (Galatians 4:10). The same verb that is duty toward God's commandments becomes bondage when attached to men's calendars.
webster_summary: To keep religiously; to obey; also, to notice or watch attentively. Scripture's dominant sense is keeping — observing to do what God commanded — while warning against an observance of days and seasons that returns a man to bondage.
webster_full: OBSERVE, v.t. [L. observo; ob and servo, to keep.] To see or behold with some attention; to notice; as, to observe a passing object.
2. To keep religiously; to celebrate; as, to observe the sabbath.
3. To keep or adhere to in practice; to comply with; to obey; as, to observe the laws of the state.
4. To remark; to express as an opinion or judgment.
OBSERVE, v.i. To be attentive; also, to remark or comment.
OBSERVANCE, n. The act of observing; performance of what is enjoined; respect; ceremonial rite.
scriptures: Ye shall observe to do therefore as the LORD your God hath commanded you: ye shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left.
And ye shall observe this thing for an ordinance to thee and to thy sons for ever.
Whoso is wise, and will observe these things, even they shall understand the lovingkindness of the LORD.
Ye observe days, and months, and times, and years.
corruption_summary: The word has faded from keep to notice, so that commands are examined rather than obeyed, while the observance Paul actually rebuked — days and seasons imposed on the conscience — is defended as devotion.
corruption_paragraphs: English usage has drained the imperative out of the word. To observe now suggests standing at a distance and taking note, and a reader who carries that sense into Deuteronomy 5:32 will hear a call to study where Moses issued a call to do. The Hebrew shamar means to guard, and the thing guarded is guarded by being performed. A religion of observation without keeping is precisely the condition our Lord condemned in men who searched the Scriptures diligently and would not come to Him, and James names it as hearing without doing, which he compares to a man who looks at his face and goes away.

The opposite corruption fills the emptied word with a calendar. Galatians 4:10 is not a rebuke of good order or of the Lord's day; it addresses Gentile believers being pressed back under a system of days and seasons as though acceptance depended on them, and Paul's alarm is that his labour on them might be in vain. Where a church binds consciences with observances God has not commanded — and the regulative principle is the safeguard here, that what Scripture has not commanded in worship is not required — observance has become the bondage it was meant to prevent.
roots_summary: Hebrew shamar (to keep, guard, watch) is the dominant word, joined to 'asah (to do); Greek tereo (to keep, guard) and paratereo (to observe scrupulously) render the New Testament senses.
roots_lines: Hebrew shamar (H8104) — to keep, guard, observe; the verb of keeping the commandments and the charge of the sanctuary.
Hebrew 'asah (H6213) — to do, make, perform; joined to shamar in “observe to do”.
Hebrew chuqqah (H2708) — a statute, an ordinance; the thing observed for ever in Exodus 12:24.
Greek tereo (G5083) — to keep, to guard, to observe; used of keeping Christ's commandments and His word.
Greek paratereo (G3906) — to observe scrupulously, to watch narrowly; the verb of Galatians 4:10.
usage: “Ye shall observe to do” — observance is defined as doing, not as noticing.
“Observe this thing for an ordinance… for ever” — observance carries truth to the children.
“Ye observe days, and months” — observance bound to men's calendars becomes bondage.

pos: v. (to think upon attentively; to ponder; rendering Hebrew bin, siym leb, Greek katanoeo)
etymology: From Latin considero, to observe the stars — literally to look at closely. Scripture commands considering as a deliberate act: of the heavens, of the lilies, of one's own ways, and above all of Christ.
biblical_def: To consider is to fix the attention deliberately, and Scripture issues it as a command with named objects. David considers the heavens and derives from them not his own significance but his smallness before the God who ordained them: “When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained” (Psalm 8:3). Haggai turns the same verb inward upon a people busy with their own houses while God's lay waste, and the command is only three words in English: “Consider your ways” (Haggai 1:5). Self-examination in Scripture is not morbid introspection but this — a deliberate audit of the way one is actually going. Our Lord directs the verb at the created order as a cure for anxiety: “And why take ye thought for raiment? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin” (Matthew 6:28). The lilies are evidence, and the considering is meant to produce a conclusion about the Father. The highest object is named by the writer to the Hebrews: “holy brethren, partakers of the heavenly calling, consider the Apostle and High Priest of our profession, Christ Jesus” (Hebrews 3:1). All other considering is preparation for that one.
webster_summary: To fix the mind on; to ponder; to think seriously upon; to regard. Scripture commands considering the heavens, the lilies, one's own ways, and chiefly Christ Jesus the Apostle and High Priest of our profession.
webster_full: CONSIDER, v.t. [L. considero, to observe attentively.] To fix the mind on, with a view to a careful examination; to think on with care; to ponder; to study; to meditate on.
2. To view attentively; to observe and examine.
3. To have regard to; to respect; as, to consider the poor.
4. To take into view in examination, or into account in estimates.
CONSIDER, v.i. To think seriously, maturely or carefully; to reflect; also, to deliberate; to turn in the mind.
CONSIDERATE, a. Given to consideration; thoughtful; serious; prudent; not hasty or rash.
scriptures: When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained;
Now therefore thus saith the LORD of hosts; Consider your ways.
And why take ye thought for raiment? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin:
Wherefore, holy brethren, partakers of the heavenly calling, consider the Apostle and High Priest of our profession, Christ Jesus;
corruption_summary: Self-examination has been replaced by self-expression, and the considering Scripture commands — a deliberate audit of one's ways against God's word — is now widely treated as unhealthy scrupulosity.
corruption_paragraphs: Haggai's three-word command is out of fashion. To consider one's ways is to compare the actual course of a life with what God requires, and the age has taught men that such comparison is unkind to the self and productive of shame. The result is a religion of expression in which a man reports his feelings at length and audits his conduct never. Scripture's command is neither morbid nor endless: it has an object (thy ways), a standard (the word of the LORD by the prophet), and an outcome (the people obeyed and built). Introspection without a standard is a maze; considering one's ways is a survey with fixed points. # voice-lock-ok: therapy: names the re-description of self-examination as 'unhealthy' in order to rebut it

A second corruption keeps considering and misdirects it. Psalm 8:3 and Matthew 6:28 both begin in creation, and modern devotion regularly stops there, turning the heavens and the lilies into occasions for a general sense of wonder detached from the God who ordained them. David's considering leads to a question about man's smallness and God's mindfulness; our Lord's leads to a conclusion about the Father's care and a rebuke of anxiety. Neither terminates on the scenery. Hebrews 3:1 names the object that governs all the rest, and a life that considers everything except Christ has not obeyed the command at all.
roots_summary: Hebrew bin (to discern, understand) and the idiom siym leb (to set the heart upon) supply the Old Testament sense; Greek katanoeo (to perceive fully, to fix the mind on) governs the New Testament commands.
roots_lines: Hebrew bin (H995) — to discern, to understand, to consider; the verb of attentive discernment throughout the Wisdom books.
Hebrew siym leb — literally to set the heart; the idiom rendered “consider your ways” in Haggai 1:5.
Hebrew ra'ah (H7200) — to see, to look at, to consider; used of David seeing the heavens in Psalm 8:3.
Greek katanoeo (G2657) — to observe fully, to fix the mind upon; the verb of Matthew 6:28 and Hebrews 3:1.
Greek logizomai (G3049) — to reckon, to account; the deliberate reckoning Paul commands concerning sin and Christ.
usage: “When I consider thy heavens” — the considering leads to a conclusion about God and man.
“Consider your ways” — self-examination has a fixed standard and a practical outcome.
“Consider the Apostle and High Priest of our profession” — Christ is the chief object of the command.

pos: v. (to take what is offered or given; to admit; rendering Hebrew laqach, Greek lambano, dechomai)
etymology: From Latin recipio, to take back or admit. Receiving is the posture of faith in Scripture: the hand that takes contributes nothing to the gift, which is why salvation is described as receiving Christ rather than achieving Him.
biblical_def: To receive is to take what another gives, and Scripture makes it the characteristic act of faith precisely because it adds nothing to the gift. John states the terms of sonship in exactly that form: “But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name” (John 1:12). Receiving and believing are set as one act, and what is received is a Person before it is a benefit. Paul makes that reception the pattern for the whole Christian life rather than merely its beginning: “As ye have therefore received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk ye in him” (Colossians 2:6). The manner of receiving governs the manner of walking, which forecloses any scheme that begins in grace and continues by works. James specifies the disposition required for receiving the word, and it is not cleverness: “receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls” (James 1:21), preceded by the laying apart of filthiness. Yet Scripture also warns against making receiving the whole of religion, recording our Lord's own saying to that effect: “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35).
webster_summary: To take, as a thing offered or sent; to accept; to admit; to embrace. Scripture makes receiving the act of faith — receiving Christ, receiving the engrafted word with meekness — while recording that it is more blessed to give than to receive.
webster_full: RECEIVE, v.t. [L. recipio; re and capio, to take.] To take, as a thing offered or sent; to accept; as, to receive a gift.
2. To take as due or as a reward; as, to receive payment or honor.
3. To take or obtain intellectually; as, to receive an opinion or a doctrine.
4. To entertain as a guest; to admit into a house or family.
5. To admit; to allow; to hold as true; as, this doctrine is generally received.
6. To take in or contain; to be able to hold; as, the vessel receives a gallon.
scriptures: But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name:
As ye have therefore received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk ye in him:
Wherefore lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness, and receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls.
I have shewed you all things, how that so labouring ye ought to support the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he said, It is more blessed to give than to receive.
corruption_summary: Receiving has been made an achievement — a decision credited to the receiver's will — so that the one word Scripture chose to exclude boasting is turned into the ground of it.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture's choice of receive is deliberate. A beggar taking bread contributes the taking and nothing else, and the word was chosen to make grace unmistakable. Much popular evangelism has managed to invert it, presenting the reception itself as the decisive human contribution — a work of the will on which everything hinges — so that a man may finally rest his assurance on the sincerity of his own act of receiving rather than on Christ received. John 1:12 forbids the reading in its own next verse, which grounds such sonship not in blood, nor in the will of the flesh, nor in the will of man, but in God.

The second corruption keeps receiving and stops there. A religion of reception alone treats Christ as a supplier of benefits and produces a hearer who is always taking in and never giving out. Paul cites a saying of the Lord Jesus against it while charging the Ephesian elders to support the weak, and James joins receiving the engrafted word with laying apart filthiness and becoming a doer of it. Colossians 2:6 settles the shape of the Christian life: as ye received Him, so walk. The walking is not a second and different principle; it is the same receiving, extended over a life.
roots_summary: Hebrew laqach (to take, receive) supplies the Old Testament sense; Greek lambano (to take, receive) governs John 1:12, and dechomai (to welcome, accept) the receiving of the word with meekness.
roots_lines: Hebrew laqach (H3947) — to take, to receive, to fetch; the ordinary verb of taking what is given.
Hebrew nasa (H5375) — to lift, to bear, to take up; used of receiving a blessing from the LORD.
Greek lambano (G2983) — to take, to receive; the verb of receiving Christ in John 1:12.
Greek dechomai (G1209) — to receive, to welcome, to accept; used of receiving the word with readiness.
Greek paralambano (G3880) — to receive from another, to receive a tradition; the verb of Colossians 2:6.
usage: “As many as received him” — receiving is faith's act, and it takes a Person.
“As ye have therefore received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk ye in him” — the walk follows the manner of receiving.
“It is more blessed to give than to receive” — a religion of receiving alone stops short.

pos: v. (to make ready beforehand; rendering Hebrew kuwn, Greek hetoimazo)
etymology: From Latin praeparo, to make ready before. Scripture's preparations run in both directions: God prepares a place, a way, and a people, and men are commanded to prepare to meet Him.
biblical_def: To prepare is to make ready in advance, and Scripture uses it of God's work and of man's duty without confusing the two. The prophet's summons is the sharpest form of the duty, and it is addressed to a people who had refused every lesser warning: “Therefore thus will I do unto thee, O Israel: and because I will do this unto thee, prepare to meet thy God, O Israel” (Amos 4:12). The meeting is certain; only the preparation is in question. The forerunner's task is stated in the same imperative mood: “The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the LORD, make straight in the desert a highway for our God” (Isaiah 40:3), which John the Baptist fulfilled by preaching repentance. Preparation of the way is repentance, not decoration. On the other side stands Christ's own preparing, which is entirely His work and the ground of the disciples' comfort: “In my Father's house are many mansions: if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you” (John 14:2). And the two meet in the vessel that is made ready for use: “If a man therefore purge himself from these, he shall be a vessel unto honour, sanctified, and meet for the master's use, and prepared unto every good work” (2 Timothy 2:21).
webster_summary: To fit, adapt, or qualify for a particular purpose; to make ready beforehand. Scripture commands men to prepare to meet God and to prepare His way by repentance, while Christ prepares a place and God prepares His vessels for use.
webster_full: PREPARE, v.t. [L. praeparo; prae, before, and paro, to get ready.] To fit, adapt or qualify for a particular purpose, end, use, service or state.
2. To make ready; as, to prepare the table; to prepare a room for a guest.
3. To provide; to procure beforehand; as, to prepare arms or provisions.
4. To set; to establish; as, the LORD hath prepared his throne in the heavens.
PREPARE, v.i. To make all things ready; to put things in suitable order; as, prepare for the reception of the enemy.
PREPARATION, n. The act of making ready beforehand; the state of being prepared; that which is prepared.
scriptures: Therefore thus will I do unto thee, O Israel: and because I will do this unto thee, prepare to meet thy God, O Israel.
The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the LORD, make straight in the desert a highway for our God.
In my Father's house are many mansions: if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you.
If a man therefore purge himself from these, he shall be a vessel unto honour, sanctified, and meet for the master's use, and prepared unto every good work.
corruption_summary: Preparation to meet God has quietly dropped out of preaching, so that death and judgment arrive as topics no one has been readied for, while the preparation of the way is mistaken for making the gospel comfortable.
corruption_paragraphs: Amos 4:12 assumes a fact the age suppresses: the meeting will occur. Every man will stand before God, and the only open question is whether he comes prepared. A ministry that never issues the summons has not thereby spared anyone; it has left them to arrive unready at an appointment they cannot miss. The older preaching was full of this and was not morbid for it — men were taught to number their days, to make their calling and election sure, and to set their house in order — and its absence is why so many now meet bereavement and their own mortality with no furniture of thought at all.

The corresponding error mistakes what preparing the way means. Isaiah 40:3 was fulfilled by a man in camel's hair preaching repentance and the remission of sins, and the levelling and straightening in the passage are moral. Where preparing the way is instead understood as removing every obstacle of offence from the gospel — smoothing the message until nothing in it can trouble a hearer — the highway is not made straight but abolished. Christ's own preparing in John 14:2 is the comfort that makes the summons bearable: the place is prepared by Him, and the preparing of the man is repentance, not renovation of the message.
roots_summary: Hebrew kuwn (to establish, make firm, prepare) and panah (to clear the way) supply the Old Testament senses; Greek hetoimazo (to make ready) governs the New Testament preparings.
roots_lines: Hebrew kuwn (H3559) — to establish, to make firm, to prepare; used of a throne prepared and a heart prepared to seek God.
Hebrew panah (H6437) — to turn, to clear away; the clearing of the way in Isaiah 40:3.
Hebrew 'arak (H6186) — to arrange, to set in order; used of preparing a table and ordering a sacrifice.
Greek hetoimazo (G2090) — to make ready, to prepare; the verb of John 14:2 and of preparing the Lord's way.
Greek katartizo (G2675) — to fit, to equip thoroughly; the perfecting of the saints unto every good work.
usage: “Prepare to meet thy God, O Israel” — the meeting is certain; readiness is not.
“Prepare ye the way of the LORD” — the preparing was done by preaching repentance.
“I go to prepare a place for you” — the place is made ready by Christ Himself.

pos: v. (to entrust or deliver in trust; also to do or perpetrate; rendering Hebrew galal, paqad, Greek paratithemi, paradidomi)
etymology: From Latin committo, to send or put together, to entrust. The English word runs two ways — a man commits a sin and commits his soul — and Scripture uses both, sending the sinner from the first to the second.
biblical_def: To commit is to hand a thing over into keeping, and Scripture builds a whole doctrine of trust upon it. The Psalmist commands the act and attaches a promise: “Commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass” (Psalm 37:5). The way is the whole course of a life, and what follows the committing is God's action rather than the man's. Proverbs applies it to labour and names the effect on the inner man: “Commit thy works unto the LORD, and thy thoughts shall be established” (Proverbs 16:3). Settled thoughts follow committed works, which is the reverse of the order anxiety proposes. Paul's confidence in prison rests on the same verb, twice over: “I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day” (2 Timothy 1:12). The object of trust is a Person known, and the deposit is safe because of His ability, not the depositor's grip. The supreme instance is our Lord's under injustice: “when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously” (1 Peter 2:23). He did not answer His accusers because He had handed the verdict to His Father.
webster_summary: To give in trust; to deliver for safe keeping; to entrust; also, to do or perpetrate, as an offence. Scripture commands committing the way, the works, and the soul to God, and shows Christ committing His cause to Him that judgeth righteously.
webster_full: COMMIT, v.t. [L. committo; con and mitto, to send.] To give in trust; to put into the hands or power of another; to entrust; as, to commit a secret to a friend.
2. To put into any place for preservation; to deposit; as, to commit a body to the grave.
3. To do; to effect or perpetrate; as, to commit murder or trespass.
4. To send to prison; to imprison by order or warrant.
5. To engage; to pledge; as, to commit one's self to a course.
COMMITMENT, n. The act of committing; a sending to prison; a deposit; an engagement.
scriptures: Commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass.
Commit thy works unto the LORD, and thy thoughts shall be established.

For the which cause I also suffer these things: nevertheless I am not ashamed: for I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day.
Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously:
corruption_summary: Commitment has been relocated from God to the self — a man's commitment to his goals, his values, his vision — so that the word which named the handing over of a life now names the tightening of a grip on it.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern usage has made commitment a quality of the will directed at one's own ends, and churches have borrowed the sense wholesale, measuring believers by their level of commitment as though the word described intensity of effort. Scripture's verb is almost the opposite motion. To commit is to hand over — the way, the works, the keeping of the soul — and what follows is expressly God's doing: he shall bring it to pass, thy thoughts shall be established, He is able to keep. A congregation exhorted to greater commitment in the modern sense is being urged to grip harder at precisely the point Scripture tells it to let go.

The second corruption is quietist and misreads the same texts. Committing the way to the LORD is not the abandonment of labour: Proverbs speaks of committing thy works, which presupposes working, and Paul committed his deposit while spending himself in ministry to the point of chains. Nor does it guarantee present vindication. 1 Peter 2:23 is the pattern under injustice — our Lord did not answer, because He had committed the case to Him that judgeth righteously, and the vindication came at the resurrection rather than at the trial. Committing is active trust that keeps working and leaves the verdict with God.
roots_summary: Hebrew galal (to roll, as a burden rolled onto another) gives Psalm 37:5 its force; paqad (to deposit, to entrust) the sense of a charge laid up; Greek paratithemi (to place beside, to deposit) governs 2 Timothy 1:12.
roots_lines: Hebrew galal (H1556) — to roll; the picture in “commit thy way” is a burden rolled off oneself onto the LORD.
Hebrew paqad (H6485) — to visit, to appoint, to deposit in trust; the word for a charge committed to another's keeping.
Greek paratithemi (G3908) — to set before, to entrust, to deposit; used of Paul's deposit kept against that day.
Greek parathēkē (G3866) — a deposit, a trust committed; the noun of the good thing committed to Timothy.
Greek paradidomi (G3860) — to give over, to deliver up; the verb of 1 Peter 2:23 for committing the cause to God.
usage: “Commit thy way unto the LORD… and he shall bring it to pass” — the committing is ours, the accomplishing His.
“He is able to keep that which I have committed unto him” — safety rests on the Keeper's ability.
“Committed himself to him that judgeth righteously” — the verdict was left with the Father.

pos: n. & v. (gain or advantage; to be of use; rendering Hebrew ya'al, bĕtsa, Greek ōpheleo, kerdos)
etymology: From Latin proficio, to go forward, to advance. Scripture is willing to reason in the language of gain and loss, and it does so to show that the largest possible profit, weighed against the soul, is a loss.
biblical_def: Profit is gain or advantage, and Scripture uses the merchant's vocabulary deliberately, reasoning with men on the ground they already understand. Our Lord poses the calculation in its most extreme form: “For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?” (Mark 8:36). He does not deny that the world is a gain; He weighs it and finds the exchange ruinous. Proverbs applies the same accounting to the day when accounts are settled: “Riches profit not in the day of wrath: but righteousness delivereth from death” (Proverbs 11:4). Riches are not called worthless generally — they are called worthless then, which is the only moment that finally prices them. The word also measures the usefulness of Scripture itself, and the list is comprehensive: “All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness” (2 Timothy 3:16). Yet even the word preached may fail of profit, and the reason given is precise: “the word preached did not profit them, not being mixed with faith in them that heard it” (Hebrews 4:2). Hearing without faith is a transaction that yields nothing.
webster_summary: Gain; advantage; any accession of good from labour or business; also, to be of use or advantage. Scripture weighs the whole world against one soul, denies that riches profit in the day of wrath, and calls all Scripture profitable to the hearer who mixes it with faith.
webster_full: PROFIT, n. [L. profectus, from proficio, to go forward.] Gain; advantage; any accession of good from labor or business; the excess of value received for producing over the cost.
2. Advantage; benefit; improvement; as, the profit of instruction.
PROFIT, v.t. To benefit; to advantage; to be of use to; as, learning profits a man.
PROFIT, v.i. To gain advantage in money or goods; also, to make improvement; to improve; to grow wiser or better.
PROFITABLE, a. Yielding or bringing profit or gain; gainful; lucrative; useful; advantageous.
PROFITLESS, a. Void of profit, gain or advantage.
scriptures: For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?
Riches profit not in the day of wrath: but righteousness delivereth from death.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
For unto us was the gospel preached, as well as unto them: but the word preached did not profit them, not being mixed with faith in them that heard it.
corruption_summary: The calculation our Lord invited has been abandoned at both ends: gain is pursued without ever being weighed against the soul, and where the weighing is attempted, the soul's loss is quietly assumed to be recoverable later.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 8:36 is a question, not a prohibition, and it presumes that a man is capable of doing arithmetic about his own life. The modern difficulty is not that men do the sum and get it wrong; it is that the sum is never attempted. A life is spent acquiring without any moment in which the acquisition is set against what it cost, and the question our Lord asked is deferred indefinitely because the day of wrath in Proverbs 11:4 is not believed to be coming. Remove that day and the arithmetic has no closing balance, at which point every gain looks like profit because nothing is ever finally priced.

The second corruption touches the profit of the word itself. Hebrews 4:2 explains a failure that ought to be impossible: the same gospel preached to two hearers, profiting one and not the other, and the difference located in faith rather than in the preaching. Where a hearer assumes that exposure to sound doctrine is itself the benefit — that attendance, familiarity, and agreement constitute profit — he may sit under the truth for decades and gain nothing by it. 2 Timothy 3:16 lists what Scripture is profitable for, and the list includes reproof and correction, which are precisely the profits an unbelieving hearer declines.
roots_summary: Hebrew ya'al (to profit, to be of use) and bĕtsa (unjust gain) mark the two sides of gain; Greek ōpheleo (to benefit, profit) and kerdaino (to gain) carry the New Testament reckoning.
roots_lines: Hebrew ya'al (H3276) — to profit, to be of use; used of idols that cannot profit and of vain things that do not deliver.
Hebrew bĕtsa' (H1215) — gain made by violence, unjust profit; the covetousness forbidden in elders.
Hebrew hown (H1952) — wealth, riches, substance; the riches that profit not in the day of wrath.
Greek ōpheleo (G5623) — to help, to benefit, to profit; the verb of Hebrews 4:2 for a word that did not profit.
Greek ōphelimos (G5624) — profitable, useful; the adjective applied to all Scripture in 2 Timothy 3:16.
usage: “What shall it profit a man… and lose his own soul?” — the largest gain is weighed and found ruinous.
“Riches profit not in the day of wrath” — wealth is priced by the day that settles accounts.
“Not being mixed with faith in them that heard it” — hearing without faith yields nothing.
